title: Pharmacotherapy I: Cardiovascular, Endocrine and Respiratory
description: Evidence-based drug therapy and pharmaceutical care for hypertension, heart failure and ischaemic heart disease, diabetes, asthma and COPD, and peptic ulcer disease.

topics.title: Hypertension Management
topics.summary: Diagnosis, targets, stepwise therapy, special populations and pharmacist counselling.

notes.b: Hypertension is diagnosed by repeated clinic BP ≥ 140/90 mmHg (confirmed by ambulatory or home monitoring where possible). Assess cardiovascular risk and target organ damage (heart, kidney, eyes, brain). Lifestyle measures: salt reduction (< 5 g/day — watch bouillon cubes), weight loss, DASH-style diet, exercise, limiting alcohol, stopping smoking. Drug therapy: for Black African patients start with a calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) or thiazide-like diuretic, often as a single-pill combination; add an ACE inhibitor/ARB, then a thiazide/CCB (A + C + D), then spironolactone or a β-blocker/α-blocker for resistant hypertension. Target generally < 140/90 mmHg, and < 130/80 in many higher-risk patients if tolerated. Compelling indications: ACEi/ARB in diabetes with albuminuria and in heart failure; β-blocker after MI; methyldopa, labetalol or nifedipine in pregnancy (avoid ACEi/ARBs).
k: Black African patients: CCB or thiazide first
Pregnancy: methyldopa, labetalol, nifedipine; no ACEi

notes.b: Poor adherence is the main cause of uncontrolled hypertension in Nigeria (cost, asymptomatic disease, side effects, belief in herbal cures). Pharmacists counsel on the lifelong nature of therapy, correct use (once-daily dosing aids adherence), side effects (ACEi cough, CCB ankle swelling, thiazide urination and gout), home BP monitoring, avoiding NSAIDs and decongestants that raise BP, and recognising hypertensive emergencies (severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness, visual loss, confusion). Monitor potassium and creatinine with ACEi/ARBs, diuretics and spironolactone. Fixed-dose combinations reduce pill burden and cost.
k: Counsel on side effects and lifelong therapy

topics.title: Heart Failure and Ischaemic Heart Disease
topics.summary: Guideline-directed therapy for heart failure, angina and acute coronary syndrome, and secondary prevention.

notes.b: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) is treated with four drug classes that reduce mortality: ACE inhibitor/ARB or sacubitril–valsartan, evidence-based β-blocker (bisoprolol, carvedilol), mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone) and SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin/empagliflozin); loop diuretics relieve congestion. Start low and titrate. Monitor weight, symptoms, BP, heart rate, potassium and renal function. Avoid drugs that worsen heart failure: NSAIDs, non-dihydropyridine CCBs (verapamil, diltiazem) in HFrEF, thiazolidinediones and excessive salt. Common causes in Nigeria include hypertensive heart disease, dilated and peripartum cardiomyopathy, and rheumatic heart disease.
k: Four pillars: ACEi/ARNI, β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i

notes.b: Stable angina: sublingual GTN for acute attacks (repeat every 5 minutes up to 3 times; seek help if unresolved), β-blockers or CCBs for prevention, plus long-acting nitrates or others as needed. Acute coronary syndrome: aspirin 300 mg chewed, a second antiplatelet (clopidogrel or ticagrelor), anticoagulation, nitrates, analgesia, oxygen if hypoxic, and reperfusion (PCI or thrombolysis — streptokinase/alteplase for STEMI when PCI unavailable). Secondary prevention: aspirin (with dual antiplatelet therapy for up to 12 months), high-intensity statin (atorvastatin 40–80 mg), β-blocker, ACE inhibitor, lifestyle change and cardiac rehabilitation. Counsel on GTN storage (original glass bottle, discard 8 weeks after opening for tablets), headache, and avoiding phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors.
k: Secondary prevention: aspirin, statin, β-blocker, ACEi

topics.title: Diabetes Mellitus Pharmacotherapy
topics.summary: Glycaemic targets, oral agents and insulin regimens, hypoglycaemia, and counselling.

notes.b: Type 1 diabetes requires insulin (basal–bolus or premixed twice-daily regimens). Type 2 diabetes: lifestyle plus metformin first-line; add a second agent based on comorbidities, cost and availability — sulphonylurea (gliclazide preferred in the elderly over glibenclamide), SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 receptor agonist (preferred in established cardiovascular or kidney disease or heart failure), DPP-4 inhibitor, pioglitazone, or insulin. Typical targets: HbA1c around 7% (53 mmol/mol) individualised; fasting glucose about 4.4–7.2 mmol/L. Manage cardiovascular risk (BP, statin), screen for complications (eyes, feet, kidneys). Metformin should be stopped temporarily during severe illness, dehydration or iodinated contrast with renal impairment; avoid if eGFR < 30.
k: SGLT2i/GLP-1 RA in CVD, CKD, HF
Gliclazide preferred over glibenclamide in elderly

notes.b: Insulin counselling: correct injection technique (subcutaneous into abdomen, thighs or arms; rotate sites to avoid lipohypertrophy), storage (unopened vials refrigerated at 2–8 °C, never frozen; in-use vials at room temperature for about 4–6 weeks — use clay-pot coolers where there is no electricity), timing with meals, and glucose self-monitoring. Hypoglycaemia (glucose < 4 mmol/L): symptoms include sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger, confusion; treat with 15–20 g fast-acting carbohydrate (glucose tablets, sugary drink) and recheck in 15 minutes ('rule of 15'), then a starchy snack; if unconscious, IV dextrose or IM glucagon. Sick-day rules: never stop insulin, monitor glucose and ketones more often, maintain fluids. Foot care education prevents amputations.
k: Unconscious: IV dextrose or IM glucagon

topics.title: Asthma and COPD
topics.summary: Stepwise asthma therapy, inhaler technique, COPD management and acute exacerbations.

notes.b: Asthma is chronic airway inflammation with variable airflow obstruction. Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS — beclometasone, budesonide, fluticasone) are the cornerstone of control. Current guidance (GINA) discourages SABA-only treatment in adults and adolescents; preferred reliever is low-dose ICS–formoterol as needed, or SABA (salbutamol) with ICS. Stepwise escalation: low-dose ICS → ICS–LABA → medium/high-dose ICS–LABA → add-on therapies (tiotropium, montelukast, biologics). Assess control (daytime symptoms, night waking, reliever use, activity limitation) and adherence and inhaler technique before stepping up. Acute severe asthma: oxygen, high-dose nebulised salbutamol (± ipratropium), oral or IV corticosteroids (prednisolone 40–50 mg), IV magnesium sulphate for severe cases. ICS side effects: oral thrush and dysphonia — rinse mouth and use a spacer.
k: Check technique and adherence before stepping up

notes.b: COPD (mainly from smoking and household biomass smoke in Nigeria) is managed with smoking cessation, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal), pulmonary rehabilitation, and bronchodilators — long-acting muscarinic antagonists (tiotropium) and/or long-acting β2 agonists; ICS is added for frequent exacerbations with high eosinophils. Exacerbations: increased bronchodilators, oral prednisolone (5 days), antibiotics if sputum is purulent, and controlled oxygen (target SpO2 88–92%). Inhaler technique for a pressurised metered-dose inhaler: shake, breathe out, seal lips, press and inhale slowly and deeply, hold breath for about 10 seconds; spacers improve delivery (essential for children and during attacks). Dry powder inhalers need a fast, deep inhalation and should not be shaken or exhaled into.
k: pMDI: slow inhalation, hold breath 10 s

topics.title: Peptic Ulcer Disease and GI Pharmacotherapy
topics.summary: H. pylori eradication, NSAID ulcers, GORD, and drugs for diarrhoea and constipation.

notes.b: The main causes of peptic ulcers are Helicobacter pylori infection (very common in Nigeria) and NSAIDs. Diagnosis of H. pylori: urea breath test, stool antigen test, or biopsy urease test (stop PPIs 2 weeks before testing). Eradication therapy (triple therapy for 14 days): a proton pump inhibitor (omeprazole or esomeprazole) plus two antibiotics — amoxicillin and clarithromycin (or metronidazole if penicillin-allergic); bismuth quadruple therapy where clarithromycin resistance is high. Confirm eradication. NSAID ulcers: stop the NSAID if possible, give a PPI; for patients who must continue NSAIDs, use gastroprotection with a PPI. Warning ('alarm') features requiring endoscopy: bleeding (haematemesis, melaena), anaemia, weight loss, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, age over ~55 with new symptoms.
k: H. pylori and NSAIDs: main causes
Triple therapy: PPI + amoxicillin + clarithromycin, 14 days
Stop PPI 2 weeks before H. pylori testing

notes.b: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: lifestyle (weight loss, avoid late meals, raise the head of the bed), antacids and alginates for symptoms, PPIs for erosive disease; long-term PPI use may cause low magnesium, B12 deficiency, C. difficile infection and fractures — review regularly. H2-receptor antagonists (famotidine) are alternatives. Diarrhoea: ORS and zinc in children; loperamide for adults with non-bloody diarrhoea (avoid in dysentery and in young children); antibiotics only for specific indications (cholera, dysentery, confirmed infections). Constipation: fluids and fibre, bulk-forming laxatives (ispaghula), osmotic laxatives (lactulose, macrogol), stimulant laxatives (senna, bisacodyl). Antiemetics: metoclopramide (extrapyramidal effects in young people), ondansetron (QT prolongation), promethazine; hyoscine for motion sickness.
k: Loperamide: avoid in dysentery and young children
